vision.title: Building more than an export business.
desc: We are not simply looking to export fruit. We are looking to increase the value created from every African harvest.

desc: Our priority is to build solid foundations. We are progressively developing a network of growers and partners who share the same standards of quality, traceability and reliability, so we can meet the expectations of international markets over the long term.

demain.title: Building today the capacity for tomorrow.

ambition.title: Going beyond exporting.
desc: In the long term, our ambition is to develop our own processing capacity, in order to create more value locally.

We see growers as essential partners in this ambition. A sustainable value chain cannot exist without shared growth with those who cultivate the produce we export.

senegal.title: Senegal, a strategic origin for tropical fruit
senegal.desc: Geographic position, maritime access, complementary seasonality and improving infrastructure are creating new opportunities for importers looking for reliable partners.

articleSenegal.b1: Why Senegal is becoming a strategic origin for tropical fruit
articleSenegal.b2: International trade in fresh fruit is changing fast. As buyers search continuously for new origins that are reliable, competitive and able to meet the rising demands of European markets, Senegal is steadily establishing itself as a strategic sourcing destination for tropical fruit.
articleSenegal.b3: Long dominated by certain regions of Latin America and Asia, the European market is now looking with growing interest at the potential of West Africa. At the heart of that shift, Senegal benefits from particularly attractive natural, logistical and commercial advantages.
articleSenegal.b5: One of Senegal's first advantages lies in its proximity to Europe. Compared with other tropical origins several weeks of sailing away, Senegal offers shorter transit times to the main European ports such as Antwerp, Rotterdam, Algeciras and Marseille.
articleSenegal.b7: For perishable produce, every day saved in transit is a significant commercial advantage.
articleSenegal.b9: Senegal also has a particularly interesting production calendar. Certain mango varieties — notably Keitt and Kent — reach the market at times when global supply is more limited.
articleSenegal.b11: At a time when retailers are looking for consistent availability throughout the year, this becomes a major selling point.
articleSenegal.b13: Over recent years, Senegal's agricultural sector has undergone significant change. Investment in:
articleSenegal.b14: has substantially raised the quality standards applied to export. Today, many operators in the sector work to requirements aligned with the expectations of European markets.
articleSenegal.b15: This professionalisation strengthens the country's credibility with international buyers.
articleSenegal.b17: While production costs are rising in several parts of the world, Senegal retains attractive competitiveness on certain products. That competitiveness does not rest on price alone. It also builds on:
articleSenegal.b18: For European importers, choosing an origin is no longer about finding the lowest price, but about identifying the best balance between quality, reliability and total cost.
articleSenegal.b20: While mango remains one of the leading exported references, Senegal's potential is not limited to a single product. International markets are also watching with interest:
articleSenegal.b21: This diversification makes it possible to build stronger partnerships and to widen commercial opportunities between growers, exporters and distributors.
articleSenegal.b22: Trust becomes the real competitive advantage
articleSenegal.b23: In modern international trade, quality alone is no longer enough. Importers now look for:
articleSenegal.b24: Senegal is seeing a new generation of export operators emerge that can meet these expectations. That shift is reinforcing the country's image as a credible long-term trading partner.
articleSenegal.b25: It also rests on the emergence of companies able to connect local growers effectively to the requirements of international markets.
articleSenegal.b26: At Tropicaura, we believe value does not lie in the product alone, but in the quality of execution, the transparency of exchanges and the ability to build lasting relationships between everyone in the supply chain.
articleSenegal.b27: Our ambition is to contribute to this new generation of African tropical trade: better structured, more reliable and more focused on the long term.
articleSenegal.b28: An opportunity that is only beginning
articleSenegal.b29: European markets' growing interest in West Africa is not a passing trend. The combination of geographic, logistical, agricultural and human factors now places Senegal among the most promising origins in international tropical trade.
articleSenegal.b30: For importers looking for new sourcing opportunities, as well as for growers seeking access to more markets, the country now has the foundations it needs to play an increasingly important role in the years ahead.
articleSenegal.b31: Senegal, an origin for the future
articleSenegal.b32: Senegal today holds many of the assets needed to become one of the reference origins in tropical trade towards Europe.
articleSenegal.b33: Its geographic proximity, its strategic seasonality, the continuous improvement of its infrastructure and the rising expertise of its operators together create an environment favourable to lasting partnerships.
articleSenegal.b34: At Tropicaura, we are convinced that the future of tropical trade rests on solid relationships between growers, exporters, logistics providers and importers.
articleSenegal.b35: Our mission is to make those connections easier, and to help develop a supply chain between Africa and Europe that is more reliable, more transparent and more effective.
articleSenegal.b36: The best opportunities arise when the right partners move in the same direction.

articleSupplier.b1: What separates a reliable supplier from an opportunistic one in West Africa
articleSupplier.b2: West Africa is attracting growing interest from international importers. The region benefits from significant agricultural potential, an advantageous geographic proximity to Europe and a steady rise in the quality standards applied to export.
articleSupplier.b3: Against that backdrop, many buyers are looking to develop new commercial relationships in order to diversify their sourcing origins and secure their volumes. Not every collaboration, however, produces the same results.
articleSupplier.b4: Some commercial relationships develop over several years and generate mutual growth. Others stop after a single season. The difference does not rest on the product alone — it usually rests on a supplier's ability to build a lasting professional relationship.
articleSupplier.b5: Reliability starts well before the first shipment
articleSupplier.b6: When an importer looks for a partner, attention naturally goes to products, prices and available volumes. Yet the strongest collaborations are usually built before the first load is even shipped.
articleSupplier.b7: The quality of those first exchanges plays an essential role:
articleSupplier.b8: The most reliable companies do not try to promise more than they can genuinely deliver. They favour realistic, transparent communication from the outset.
articleSupplier.b10: In international trade, it is relatively easy to announce large volumes, competitive prices or ambitious lead times. The real difference appears once operations begin.
articleSupplier.b11: A reliable supplier is able to:
articleSupplier.b12: Conversely, problems often arise when the expectations created at the start do not match operational reality. Trust is built through execution far more than through promises.
articleSupplier.b13: Consistency is often worth more than one excellent season
articleSupplier.b14: Trade in fresh produce depends on many factors: weather, harvests, logistics, packaging availability, transport conditions. In that environment, perfection does not exist.
articleSupplier.b15: Experienced buyers know they are not necessarily looking for a perfect partner. They are looking for a partner able to sustain a consistent level of performance over time.
articleSupplier.b16: Consistency then becomes a major competitive advantage. A stable relationship across several seasons generally creates more value than one exceptional operation followed by irregular results.
articleSupplier.b18: International supply chains always carry a degree of uncertainty. Port delays, weather constraints, market swings or logistical difficulties can arise at any time. How those situations are handled directly shapes the quality of the commercial relationship.
articleSupplier.b19: The most valued partners are often those who:
articleSupplier.b20: Transparency allows each party to anticipate risks rather than simply absorb them.
articleSupplier.b21: A long-term view changes the nature of the partnership
articleSupplier.b22: The best-performing collaborations do not rest on a transaction. They rest on a shared vision. When growers, exporters, logistics providers and importers work with a long-term mindset, the benefits reach far beyond any single operation.
articleSupplier.b24: In a sector where human relationships remain fundamental, this dimension becomes particularly important.
articleSupplier.b25: The evolution of international trade favours reliable partners
articleSupplier.b26: European markets are changing. Requirements around quality, traceability, regulatory compliance and logistical visibility are becoming increasingly important. In that context, companies able to offer:
articleSupplier.b27: are progressively strengthening their market position. Reliability is becoming a differentiator as important as the product itself.
articleSupplier.b28: At Tropicaura, we believe lasting partnerships are built around a simple idea: creating value for everyone in the supply chain.
articleSupplier.b29: Our ambition is to help develop commercial relationships founded on trust, transparency and operational excellence.
articleSupplier.b30: We are convinced that the future of African tropical trade will rest as much on the quality of the produce as on the quality of the relationships that carry it.
articleSupplier.b31: Reliability as the foundation for growth
articleSupplier.b32: In an increasingly demanding international environment, reliability is becoming a strategic asset.
articleSupplier.b33: Suppliers able to build lasting relationships, deliver on their commitments rigorously and communicate transparently create the conditions for solid, sustainable growth.
articleSupplier.b34: Beyond volumes, prices or seasons, it is often these qualities that separate the partnerships that last from those that quickly disappear.
articleSupplier.b35: The strongest commercial relationships are not built on one successful transaction. They are built on the ability to succeed together, season after season.

seo.title: Quality & Compliance — Inspections, Traceability, Export Documents
seo.description: How Tropicaura selects, inspects and documents its fresh fruit and vegetables before export: quality control, cold chain, traceability, export certificates.

quality.title: Quality is built before the harvest, not at the moment of shipping.
quality.intro: An international buyer doesn't judge an exporter on a photo, but on the consistency of what they receive, shipment after shipment. Here is how we work.

approach.heading: Our quality approach
approach.intro: Most of a shipment's quality is decided before harvest: choice of producer, monitoring through the season, timing of the pick.
points: Producers selected for consistency and their ability to meet agreed specifications
Fields monitored throughout the season, not only at harvest time
Harvest timed to match transit duration and destination market
Quality requirements communicated upfront to every partner producer

control.heading: Quality control
control.intro: Every batch is inspected before loading, not only checked as it leaves the field.
points: Visual inspection: appearance, colour, presence of defects
Ripeness and firmness checks appropriate to the product
Sorting and sizing to match the destination market's requirements
Final inspection immediately before loading

phytosanitary.heading: Phytosanitary compliance
phytosanitary.intro: Exporting fresh produce is governed by rules that are specific to each destination country.
points: Our produce is GlobalGAP certified, guaranteeing compliance with internationally recognised good agricultural practices
Phytosanitary certificate issued by the relevant authorities for every shipment that requires one
Compliance checked against the importing country's requirements before loading
Official inspections carried out in line with applicable regulations

coldChain.heading: Cold chain
coldChain.intro: Freshness is rarely lost all at once — it is lost break by break in the temperature chain. We work to limit those breaks.
points: Pre-cooling when the product and transit time require it
Storage at the appropriate temperature before loading
Temperature monitored throughout sea or air transport
Transport mode chosen according to the product's sensitivity

traceability.heading: Traceability
traceability.intro: If a question ever comes up about a shipment, we need to be able to trace it back to its origin.
points: Origin identified for every batch
Batch tracked from intake to shipment
Related documentation kept on file and available on request

documents.heading: Documents provided
documents.intro: Depending on destination and product, a shipment may include:
items: Other documents specific to the importing country's requirements

faq.q: Do you work with certified producers?
faq.a: Yes — all our produce is GlobalGAP certified, guaranteeing compliance with internationally recognised good agricultural practices.

faq.q: How do you control quality before shipping?
faq.a: Every batch goes through visual inspection, ripeness and firmness checks, sorting and sizing, then a final inspection right before loading.

faq.q: What documents do you provide with each shipment?
faq.a: Depending on destination: Phytosanitary Certificate, Commercial Invoice, Packing List, and Certificate of Origin when required by the importing country.

faq.q: How is freshness preserved during transport?
faq.a: Through pre-cooling when needed, storage at the right temperature, and cold chain monitoring throughout sea or air transport.

incoterms.heading: Incoterms
incoterms.intro: We offer several Incoterms, to be defined according to your logistics setup.

items.name: EXW
items.desc: You take charge of transport from collection at our facility.

items.name: FOB Dakar
items.desc: We handle export up to loading on board at the Port of Dakar.

items.name: CIF
items.desc: We arrange transport and insurance to the agreed destination port.

transport.heading: Transport
transport.intro: The choice between sea and air depends on the product, the volume and the timeline you need.

air.heading: Air freight
air.text: Suited to perishable products, smaller volumes or tight deadlines.

sea.heading: Sea freight
sea.text: Suited to larger volumes and products that tolerate longer transit, with cold chain management in a refrigerated container.

packaging.heading: Packaging
packaging.intro: Packaging is designed to protect the product all the way to its final destination.
points: Cartons suited to the product and the mode of transport
Palletisation following destination market standards
Protection against impact and temperature variation
Preparation adjusted to the customer's specifications

leadTimes.heading: Lead times
leadTimes.text: Lead times vary depending on destination, season and carrier availability. We provide a precise estimate for each order rather than a generic figure that wouldn't be reliable.

faq.q: Do you use air or sea freight?
faq.a: Both. Sea freight suits larger volumes and products that tolerate longer transit; air freight suits perishable products or tight deadlines.

faq.q: What are your delivery lead times?
